title.en: A story of numbers: counting, bases and place value

text.en: Reema finds a strange paper with wedge-shaped symbols. Her father says it comes from Mesopotamia about 4000 years ago, and tells her how humans learned to write numbers.

Even in the Stone Age people needed to count food, animals and trade, so they matched each animal with a stick or a pebble.
This pairing, where no two objects share the same stick, is called one-to-one mapping and it is the basis of counting.
Another method uses a fixed order of sounds or names, like the letters of a language, to name each count.
Tally marks and Roman numerals show how different cultures wrote numbers with symbols and rules of grouping.
Large numbers need grouping, so many systems use a base, like base 10 (ten of one place make one of the next place) or base 60 in Mesopotamia.
The Indian system uses ten symbols 0 to 9 where each digit has an absolute value and a place value, and a zero holds a place when it is empty.
This system made arithmetic easy, and scholars like Al-Khwarizmi carried it to the Arab world, from where Europe learned it.
Europeans called the numerals Arabic, but Arab scholars called them Hindu numerals, which is why the name Hindu-Arabic or Indian numerals is used today.
A number like 345 means 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 5 × 1, so the place of a digit decides its value.
The same idea works in any base: in base 2, only the digits 0 and 1 are used and each place is a power of 2.

Find the largest power of 2 not more than 13: 8.
13 − 8 = 5. The next power 4 fits: 5 − 4 = 1. Then 2 does not fit and 1 fits.

why.en: Use each power once or not at all.
Write 1 for powers used and 0 for powers skipped.

prompt.en: How does a place-value system help us compare with tally marks?

requiredIdeas.en: Tally marks need one mark per object.
Place value uses a few symbols for any number.
A zero shows an empty place.

commonMisconceptions.en: The value of a digit never depends on its place.

points.en: Counting began by one-to-one mapping with sticks or pebbles.
A base groups objects; we use base 10 with the digits 0 to 9.
Place value and zero made the Indian numerals powerful and they spread to the world.
